pros: Guaranteed O(log n) height — strictest balance among all self-balancing BSTs
Faster lookups than Red-Black trees due to stricter balance (1.44 vs 2.0 log n)
All operations (search, insert, delete) are O(log n) worst-case
Self-balancing: no degenerate O(n) cases unlike standard BST
Only one rotation needed after insertion (efficient)
Can be augmented for order statistics, range queries, and intervals
Deterministic performance — no randomization or amortized analysis needed
Well-understood and widely taught in computer science
Foundation for more complex tree structures
Excellent for applications with high lookup-to-update ratio
Provides sorted iteration in O(n) via in-order traversal
cons: More rotations than Red-Black trees during deletions (up to O(log n))
Each node must store height or balance factor (2 bytes overhead per node)
Slower insertions and deletions than Red-Black trees due to stricter balance
Recursive implementation can cause stack overflow on very deep trees
Not cache-friendly: pointer chasing leads to poor memory locality
Higher constant factors than simple BST for small n
More complex to implement correctly than standard BST
Not suitable for disk-based storage (use B-trees instead)
Thread-safety requires locking entire paths (difficult to parallelize)
Rebalancing after deletion is more complex than insertion
No guaranteed amortized bounds like Splay trees
Memory fragmentation from many small node allocations
